notes: Post-judgment slip rule application; Chadwick and Sedley LJ held CPR 40.12 cannot reopen interest or litigant-in-person costs not raised before sealing.

enrichment.short_title: Slip rule refusal to add interest and CPR 48.6 costs after appeal

statutes_considered.title: Litigants in Person (Costs and Expenses) Act 1975

key_facts: Roadrunner Properties appealed successfully against Dean and Suffolk and Essex Joinery over party wall damage; judgment for £1,740 was entered on 21 November 2003.
Counsel agreed an order by email and it was sealed on 2 December 2003 without orders for pre-judgment interest or explicit CPR 48.6 litigant-in-person costs.

The appellant later applied under CPR 40.12 to add statutory interest from February 2001 and CPR 48.6 costs where the company had acted through solicitors on the record but Mr Morgan appeared at trial.
The respondents offered only limited compromise on interest and disputed the costs amendments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under CPR 40.12 (the slip rule) to amend a perfected Court of Appeal order following a successful property damage appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; applicant ordered to pay respondents' costs of £933.50, set off against other costs orders.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 40.12 permits correction only where an order fails to give effect to the court's intention at the time it was made; it does not allow parties to raise points not argued before perfection, such as pre-judgment interest or litigant-in-person costs under CPR 48.6, which remain matters for detailed assessment.
legal_issues: Scope of CPR 40.12 to amend a perfected order
Whether pre-judgment interest could be added where not requested at judgment
Whether a company with solicitors on the record can recover CPR 48.6 litigant-in-person costs
Whether questions about director advocacy at trial can be raised on a slip application
linked_authorities: Bristol-Myers Squibb v Baker Norton Pharmaceuticals Inc [2001] EWCA Civ 414

confidence.notes: Outcome and CPR analysis are explicit. Some trial-level costs questions were expressly left for assessment.

notes: Family resulting-trust dispute over council house purchase contribution; trial judge's loan finding upheld on appellate fact review.

enrichment.short_title: Family dispute over beneficial interest in council house purchase
key_facts: Brothers disputed ownership of 49 Navestock Crescent after their parents' deaths; the elder son claimed he funded the 1990 right-to-buy purchase expecting the home would be his.
The trial judge found the £11,168.80 contribution was a loan, not an acquisition of beneficial interest, and ordered repayment of £10,168.80 after one alleged repayment.
The claimant had originally been named as purchaser but was removed from the title; conveyancing documents did not describe the payment as a loan.
The Court of Appeal expressed concern about the judge's reasoning but declined to overturn his credit and fact findings after a four-day trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a four-day County Court trial on beneficial ownership and repayment of funds advanced for a council house purchase.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on liability; addendum dismissed the costs cross-appeal; judgment for £10,168.80 with set-off against costs payable by the appellant.
enrichment.ratio: An appellate court will not reverse a trial judge's crucial finding of fact unless it exceeds the generous ambit within which reasonable disagreement is possible; proof the advance was a loan defeats resulting trust and common-intention trust claims even where resulting-trust principles received limited attention at trial.
legal_issues: Whether a son's cash contribution to his parents' council house purchase created a resulting or constructive trust
Whether the contribution was a loan rather than acquisition of beneficial interest
Appellate review of fact findings where witness evidence was unclear and given through an interpreter
Costs where the claimant partially succeeded on the loan repayment claim

Piglovski v Piglovska [1999] 1 W.L.R. 1360
SS Hontestroom v SS Sagaporak [1927] A.C. 37

confidence.notes: Core trust and appellate fact principles are clear. Ward LJ's doubts about the loan finding do not alter the formal outcome.

notes: Costs-only appeal after refusal of renewed JR permission; Mount Cook Land Practice Direction 8.6 applied and summary assessment ordered.

enrichment.short_title: JR permission costs after Mount Cook Land guidance
key_facts: Mr Payne sought to quash planning permission for change of use to a waste transfer and recycling facility; a deputy judge refused renewed permission on six grounds.
The deputy judge ordered the claimant to pay about £4,640 costs on detailed assessment without hearing submissions on summary versus detailed assessment.
The council attended through leading counsel at the renewed permission hearing; the appellant relied on CPR Part 54 Practice Direction paragraphs 8.5 and 8.6.
The Court of Appeal applied R (Mount Cook Land Ltd) v Westminster City Council and held the wrong costs test had been applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against costs order only, following refusal of renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; deputy judge's costs order quashed; costs of £400 ordered in favour of the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR Part 54 Practice Direction 8.6, a defendant who attends and successfully resists a renewed permission hearing should generally not recover costs from the claimant save in exceptional circumstances; where the judge applied the wrong test the costs discretion must be exercised afresh, and a one-day permission hearing with modest costs claimed warranted summary assessment.
legal_issues: Application of Practice Direction 8.6 to renewed JR permission hearings
Whether attendance by defended counsel at permission stage justified a costs order
Whether costs should have been summarily assessed
Distinction between Part 52 and Part 54 costs practice
index_terms: Guide to Summary Assessment of Costs 2002
linked_authorities: R (Mount Cook Land Ltd) v Westminster City Council [2003] EWCA Civ 1346

confidence.notes: Costs-only appeal with explicit Mount Cook Land application and clear final order.

notes: Patent claim 1 construction for ultrasonic sifting device; declarations of non-infringement granted for spiral and single bent rod designs.

enrichment.short_title: Patent non-infringement for single-rod ultrasonic screen resonators
key_facts: Russell Finex sought declarations of non-infringement of Telsonic's EP (UK) 0652810 for ultrasonic sifting devices using tuned resonator rods.
Claim 1 required rod-type resonators in the plural or at least one circular rod; Telsonic conceded a single straight rod did not infringe.
Telsonic argued spiral and single bent rod designs infringed literally or under purposive construction; Russell Finex proposed three alternative designs.
Laddie J declined to use prosecution history as an aid to construction and rejected file wrapper estoppel without binding authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court action for declarations of non-infringement of a European patent relating to ultrasonic screening equipment.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations of non-infringement granted for the Spiral and Single Bent Rod designs; literal and purposive infringement arguments rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Claim 1's requirement for multiple rod-type resonators or a circular rod is an effective limitation that cannot be read away by purposive construction merely because alternative shapes work technically; a spiral is not circular and a single bent rod is not plural rod-type resonators, and where the skilled reader cannot conclude the patentee intended to exclude such variants the limitation stands.
legal_issues: Construction of 'rod-type resonators' and 'at least one circular rod' in claim 1
Literal versus purposive infringement under Catnic and Improver
Use of claim reference numerals and prosecution history in construction
Whether spiral and single bent rod resonator designs fall within the claim

notes: Service out of Russia appeal; claimant failed to prove Arbitrazh Procedural Code applied and timely personal service under Russian law.

enrichment.short_title: Setting aside service out on Russian director in fraud claim

statutes_considered.title: Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters 1965
Arbitrazh Procedural Code of the Russian Federation
Code of Civil Procedure of the Russian Federation

key_facts: Arros Invest, in liquidation, sued former directors for alleged diversion of about $4.9 million from an oil trading fraud funded by Tatneft.

Permission to serve Mr Nishanov out of the jurisdiction was granted and the claim form expired on 17 March 2003; documents were posted to his registered Russian address and signed for by a babysitter on 13 March 2003.
Mr Nishanov did not personally receive the claim form until 19 March 2003, after expiry; he applied to set aside service and challenge jurisdiction.
Expert evidence conflicted on whether Russian service rules required personal service under the CPC or permitted postal service under the APC.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a master's decision setting aside service out of the jurisdiction and refusing extension of the claim form's validity.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; service held invalid because the claimant did not prove the APC applied or that service complied with applicable Russian procedural law in time.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties agree service did not comply with the general Russian Civil Procedure Code, a claimant relying on specialist Arbitrazh procedural rules must prove by expert evidence that those rules would govern equivalent proceedings in Russia; without such evidence, and where receipt by the defendant after expiry is common ground, postal service to a registered but non-residential address signed by an unauthorised person does not establish valid service.
legal_issues: Whether Russian Arbitrazh or civil procedure codes governed service of the claim
Validity and timing of service by registered post under Russian law
Whether signature by a babysitter constituted adequate confirmation of receipt
Whether service at registered address sufficed when defendant did not reside there
index_terms: Bumper Corporation v Commissioner of Police
linked_authorities: Bumper Corporation v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [1991] 1 WLR 1362

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome is clear though some Russian law points were not finally decided because APC applicability failed on the evidence.

notes: Long ancillary relief judgment with detailed MP Farm findings; asset division and parental occupation rights are clear but schedules are dense.

enrichment.short_title: Ancillary relief after dispute over MP Farm and joint property portfolio
key_facts: After a 15-year marriage ending in 1998, cross-applications for ancillary relief were contested over jewellery business, solicitor partnership, and extensive joint property holdings.
MP Farm was bought in 1992 in joint names to save the wife's parents' home from receivers; the wife claimed the husband promised to transfer his share to her sister.
Costs exceeded £570,000 against assets of roughly £1.1–1.4 million; the court criticised disproportionate litigation and excessive bundles.
Baron J found Mr and Mrs H had no beneficial interest in MP Farm but retained informal rights to live and run the chicken business, discounting the property value accordingly.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Seven-day final hearing of cross-applications for ancillary relief following long-running financial remedy proceedings since 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Joint assets divided equally with specified transfers including the former matrimonial home and MP Farm to the wife and The C properties and development land to the husband; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: On the facts, MP Farm was held legally and beneficially by the spouses subject to an informal agreement allowing the wife's parents to remain; parents who did not act to their detriment and could not have had a beneficial interest without defrauding creditors acquired neither constructive trust nor proprietary estoppel rights; equal division of joint assets was fair without adjusting separate businesses or pensions.
legal_issues: Beneficial ownership of MP Farm and alleged agreement to transfer to the wife's sister
Whether the wife's parents had constructive trust or proprietary estoppel rights
Valuation discount for parents' occupation rights
Fair division of jointly held property and treatment of separate businesses

notes: Leading conjoined IAT fact-appeal judgment on finality and Jeyachandran Sri Lankan Tamil guidance; all four individual appeals dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: IAT fact appeals and Jeyachandran Tamil asylum guidance
key_facts: Four conjoined appeals concerned Tamil asylum seekers from Sri Lanka whose Adjudicator decisions were overturned by the Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
The court addressed how far the IAT may overturn Adjudicators' fact findings and how Jeyachandran's 'exceptionality' guidance applied post-ceasefire.
In each case the IAT concluded improved country conditions meant return was safe except for exceptional cases such as wanted persons.
Section 101 of the 2002 Act later limited IAT appeals to points of law for post-June 2003 determinations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined appeals to the Court of Appeal against IAT decisions allowing the Secretary of State's appeals from Adjudicator determinations granting asylum and Article 3 protection.
enrichment.outcome: All four appeals dismissed; section 11 order against the Legal Services Commission; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: An open-ended IAT fact appeal requires the appellant to show objective grounds that a different view from the Adjudicator's is the right one, reflecting the public interest in finality rather than mere disagreement; where the IAT has given authoritative country guidance such as Jeyachandran, it may legitimately substitute its decision if the Adjudicator departed without good reason.
legal_issues: Constraints on the IAT when overturning Adjudicators' fact findings
Effect of Jeyachandran on Tamil Sri Lankan return cases
Distinction between error and mere disagreement on appeal
Whether failure to refer to Jeyachandran justified IAT intervention

notes: Domestic violence spouse without public funds; council appeal allowed on s21 NAA approach but s2 LGA largely blocked by s21(1A).

enrichment.short_title: Local authority duties to abused spouse without public funds

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Mrs Khan, a Pakistani national with no recourse to public funds, fled serious domestic violence and kidnapping by her husband after joining him in Oxford.
Oxfordshire refused residential accommodation under section 21 NAA and financial support under section 2 LGA, treating her need as housing destitution rather than care and attention.
Moses J quashed the section 21 decision but held section 21(1A) barred use of section 2 for accommodation and most financial assistance.
By the hearing Mrs Khan had obtained indefinite leave to remain, making the outcome largely academic but of general importance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from judicial review of a local authority's refusal of accommodation and financial support to a domestic violence victim subject to immigration control.
enrichment.outcome: Council's appeal allowed on section 21; cross-appeal dismissed except that section 2(4)(b) and (f) may provide non-accommodation assistance not prohibited by section 21(1A); declaration to be agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Domestic violence may in principle make a person's need for care and attention more acute beyond mere destitution, but the council's conclusion that it did not on these facts was not Wednesbury unreasonable; section 21(1A) is a prohibition within section 3 LGA preventing circumvention of NAA restrictions on accommodation and related payments, though section 2 remains available for assistance such as goods or services not constituting residential accommodation under section 21(5).
legal_issues: Whether domestic violence can make need for care and attention acute under section 21 NAA
Whether section 21(1A) restricts section 2 LGA powers
Scope of 'accommodation' in section 21(5)
Whether Human Rights Act section 3 requires a narrow reading of section 21(1A)

notes: IBM WEBSPHERE CTM infringement succeeded against Web-Sphere Ltd; own-name defence and malicious falsehood claim failed.

enrichment.short_title: IBM WEBSPHERE Community trade mark infringement by Web-Sphere

statutes_considered.title: Council Regulation (EC) No 40/94 on the Community trade mark

key_facts: IBM registered the Community word mark WEBSPHERE for software and related services and had traded under WebSphere since May 1998.
Publiweb Ltd changed its name to Web-Sphere Ltd in June 1999 and used hyphenated domain names for internet and later software services.
IBM sued for infringement under Article 9(1)(a) and (b) and for malicious falsehood over leaflets distributed at IBM events alleging improper registration.
Lewison J held the hyphen was insignificant, goods and services were identical or similar, and the honest own-name defence did not apply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trade mark infringement and malicious falsehood claim following pre-action correspondence from 2000.
enrichment.outcome: Trade mark infringement established against Web-Sphere Ltd and personal defendants; malicious falsehood claim failed for lack of likely pecuniary damage.
enrichment.ratio: WEBSPHERE and Web-Sphere are identical for Article 9(1)(a) purposes where the hyphen is insignificant to the average consumer and the defendant's services match the registered classes; a company that changes its name after IBM's mark and publicity cannot rely on Article 12 own-name use where the name was chosen to trade on IBM's goodwill and honest practices are lacking.
legal_issues: Whether Web-Sphere is identical or confusingly similar to WEBSPHERE
Validity of WEBSPHERE registration under Article 7 descriptiveness grounds
Application of Article 12 own-name defence to a renamed company
Whether leaflets amounted to malicious falsehood causing likely pecuniary damage

notes: CCRC reference after Preddy; s15 convictions quashed and substituted with s1 Theft Act 1978; Smith No 1 jurisdiction preferred over Manning.

enrichment.short_title: CCRC reference substituting obtaining services after Preddy
key_facts: Wallace Duncan Smith was convicted of fraudulent trading and two counts of obtaining property by deception over back-to-back repo transactions totalling about US$37 million.
On a Criminal Cases Review Commission reference, counts 3 and 4 could not stand after R v Preddy because the bank's money was paid into a New York account.
The Crown sought substitution with obtaining services by deception under section 1 Theft Act 1978, treating the repo as secured lending services.
The court preferred Smith No 1 over Manning on jurisdiction where deception occurred in England though funds were received abroad.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission treated as a further appeal under section 9 Criminal Appeal Act 1995 after prior unsuccessful appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Convictions on counts 3 and 4 quashed and substituted with section 1 Theft Act 1978 convictions; six-year concurrent sentences unchanged; count 1 not challenged after Lambert.
enrichment.ratio: Following Preddy, back-to-back repo dishonesty may be substituted as obtaining services by deception where the indictment particulars implicitly covered the financial arrangement; English courts may retain jurisdiction over obtaining offences where substantial criminal activity occurred here even if the last act occurred abroad, following the broader approach in Smith No 1 rather than Manning's strict terminatory rule.
legal_issues: Whether section 3 Criminal Appeal Act 1968 permits substitution of section 1 1978 offences for section 15 1968 convictions
Whether a repo transaction constitutes obtaining services by deception
Territorial jurisdiction where deception is in England but money is received abroad
Whether a CCRC reference can revisit issues decided on a prior appeal
